 opened October in the spotlight after unveiling a redesigned Copilot that stitches integrated Office tools, chat, collaborative workflows and automation into a single assistant, arriving as the technology group steadied alongside a firmer Nasdaq Composite. The refresh lands at a moment when cooler inflation data has eased expectations for further rate increases, lending a calmer tone to large-cap technology names across the US market. Microsoft entered October with attention fixed on its redesigned Copilot experience, which folds integrated Office tools, chat, collaborative workflows and automation features into a single assistant layer. The rollout arrived as the technology group steadied alongside a firmer Nasdaq Composite, where chip-related sentiment helped stabilize the wider software complex at the start of the month. The timing carries weight because the refreshed assistant stitches together many of the surfaces that already sit inside everyday work software. By weaving generative features directly into documents, spreadsheets, meetings and messaging, Microsoft has aimed to make the assistant feel less like a bolt-on and more like a native part of how people draft, summarize and organize a working day. Framing the refresh as a single, unified layer also sends a signal about direction. Rather than scatter assistant features across separate apps, the company has tried to present one coherent helper that moves with the user from inbox to document to meeting, a design choice that speaks to how it wants the brand understood across its customer base. A bluechip label is typically reserved for large, established names with long operating histories, broad product reach and recognizable brands. Microsoft fits that frame as one of the most widely tracked members of the S&P 500, with businesses spanning cloud computing, productivity software, gaming and devices. Within the broader Bluechip Stocks universe, the company stays closely watched across the US equity market. Firms carrying this designation tend to draw steady attention because their scale allows them to weather shifting market moods better than smaller peers. That resilience does not remove volatility, but it does give large-cap technology names a central role in how the wider market behaves day to day. For a company of this heft, membership in the bluechip tier also shapes expectations. Market watchers tend to look for consistency and breadth rather than dramatic swings, and that steadier lens colors how each fresh development is received. Microsoft runs a diversified set of operations. Its cloud arm, anchored by Azure, provides computing power, storage and services to organizations of many sizes. The productivity segment houses the familiar suite of word processing, spreadsheet, presentation and communication tools now threaded with assistant features. Beyond the cloud and productivity pillars, the company operates a gaming division built around its console and subscription offerings, along with devices and a search-and-advertising presence. This spread means no single product line defines the entire enterprise, which helps smooth the effect of swings in any one area. The reported stance that the gaming hardware unit is not being sold underscored how the company continues to treat entertainment as a lasting part of its portfolio rather than a segment to shed. That signal matters because it clarifies how management views the breadth of the franchise at a moment when many large firms are sharpening focus. Each of these arms feeds the others. Cloud capacity supports assistant features inside productivity tools, gaming services lean on the same data-center backbone, and devices act as entry points into the wider ecosystem, creating a web of connections that reinforces the whole. The assistant refresh sits inside a wider shift across the sector toward generative tooling. Chip demand commentary from a major memory maker helped steady semiconductor names as October opened, and that steadiness tends to ripple into software firms that depend on advanced processors to train and run large models. At the same time, headlines around model safety and a reported pause in some advanced training work kept the mood mixed. For a company building assistant features into widely used software, the balance between rapid capability gains and careful deployment has become a defining theme of the moment. That balance is not only technical. How assistant features are governed, explained and controlled shapes how comfortable large organizations feel leaning on them for sensitive work, which in turn influences how quickly the tools spread through the enterprise world. Supporting assistant features at scale requires enormous computing capacity, and Microsoft has signaled plans to expand its data-center footprint substantially over the coming years. Building that infrastructure demands heavy capital commitment, and market watchers have weighed that spending against the pace at which organizations adopt the new tools. The tension is straightforward to describe without numbers: more capacity can support faster cloud expansion, yet it also lifts near-term costs. How quickly demand catches up to that build-out remains a central question that the company addresses as it reports results through the year. Scale in infrastructure can also become a durable advantage. A deep and widely distributed network of data centers lets the company serve customers close to where they operate, a quality that matters as assistant features move from novelty to everyday utility. The S&P 500 edged higher to begin October after a softer inflation reading, closing out a September that ranked among the weaker ones in recent memory. Cooler price data eased expectations for further rate increases, a shift that often lends support to large-cap technology names whose earnings sit further out in time. Against that macro frame, Microsoft traded as part of a broad reset in sentiment. The steadier tone across chips, paired with a calmer read on inflation, created a backdrop in which marquee software names could regain footing after a choppy stretch. Macro conditions do not move a company of this size on their own, yet they set the stage on which company-specific news plays out. A calmer rate picture tends to make the market more receptive to the long-dated promise embedded in cloud and assistant growth. Microsoft competes across several fronts at once. In the cloud, it faces other hyperscale providers racing to add capacity and services. In productivity, rival suites and newer assistant-first tools press on the same workflows. In gaming, established console makers and subscription platforms vie for the same households. This many-sided rivalry shapes how the company directs its effort and prices its offerings. The assistant refresh can be read in part as an answer to that pressure, an effort to deepen the reasons customers stay inside its ecosystem rather than drift toward competing tools. Competition also keeps the pace of change brisk. Each advance from a rival tends to draw a response, and that back-and-forth has accelerated as assistant features move to the center of how software firms distinguish themselves. Large technology firms operate under close regulatory watch across many regions, and Microsoft is no exception. Scrutiny of market reach, data handling and the bundling of assistant features into dominant software can shape how quickly new capabilities roll out. Adoption is the other open question. Embedding assistant features broadly does not guarantee that organizations will lean on them heavily. The gap between availability and everyday use is one that the company works to close through design, pricing and demonstrated usefulness inside real tasks. Both threads tend to move slowly and matter greatly. Regulatory frameworks evolve over long stretches, while adoption builds habit by habit, and together they frame how the assistant era actually unfolds inside large organizations. With a results update expected later in the month, the company's operational focus has centered on showing that its cloud momentum and assistant features translate into durable demand. Each reporting cycle gives the market a fresh read on how the many segments are tracking. For a bluechip of this size, the emphasis tends to fall on breadth and consistency rather than any single surprise. Steady execution across cloud, productivity and gaming is what keeps the name anchored in the large-cap conversation. Commentary that accompanies results often carries as much weight as the figures themselves. How management describes demand, capacity and the pace of assistant uptake can shape the mood across the wider software group for weeks. Threading generative features through those familiar surfaces means the new helper meets people where they already spend the working day. This reach also lends the company a measure of stability. Because so many routines depend on its software, demand tends to be sticky, and that stickiness is one reason the name sits so firmly in the large-cap tier even through choppier stretches for the wider market. A large share of the company's software now reaches customers through subscriptions rather than one-off sales. That model lends a recurring quality to demand, smoothing the peaks and troughs that pure license sales once brought and giving the business a steadier rhythm across the year. Assistant features fit neatly into this frame. By adding capability to subscriptions people already pay for, the company deepens the value of each plan and strengthens the reasons customers renew, a dynamic that reinforces the durability of the wider franchise. The pace at which Microsoft ships new capability has quickened as assistant tooling has moved to the center of the sector. Frequent updates keep the software fresh and give customers reasons to stay engaged, while also setting a brisk tempo that rivals must match across cloud and productivity alike. Sustaining that cadence calls for steady spending on talent and infrastructure. Balancing the drive to innovate against the discipline of managing a sprawling enterprise is a defining task for a company of this scale as the assistant era matures. Microsoft serves customers in nearly every region, from individual users to the largest enterprises and public bodies. That global spread diversifies where demand comes from, so softness in one market can be balanced by steadiness in another, lending the franchise a broad and resilient base. A wide customer base also feeds a virtuous loop. The more organizations standardize on the company's tools, the more its ecosystem becomes a default choice for partners and developers, reinforcing the reach that underpins its bluechip standing across the market. As assistant features handle more sensitive work, the question of trust has moved to the fore. Enterprises weigh how data is protected, how features are controlled and how transparently tools behave before leaning on them for critical tasks, and a strong record here can become a genuine point of difference. Microsoft has leaned into that theme, framing security and governance as central to how its assistant layer is built. For large organizations weighing where to place trust, that emphasis can matter as much as raw capability when deciding how far to adopt the new tools. A broad web of partners and developers surrounds Microsoft's platforms, building tools and services that extend the reach of its software. That community acts as a force multiplier, widening what the ecosystem can do far beyond what any single company could build alone and deepening the reasons customers stay. Assistant features add a fresh layer to that collaboration. As partners weave the new capabilities into their own offerings, the helper spreads into more corners of daily work, reinforcing the central place the company holds across the technology landscape as the quarter unfolds. title: MSFT Stock Gains After Microsoft Grows India Cloud Footprint In Battle With Google Cloud, AWS - Stocktwits
content: Shares of Microsoft (MSFT) edged higher Thursday morning after the company announced its fourth cloud region in India and its largest data center deployment in the country to date, intensifying an infrastructure race with Alphabet’s (GOOG, GOOGL) Google Cloud and Amazon Web Services (AWS). The new India South Central cloud region, located in Hyderabad, is part of Microsoft's broader $20.5 billion investment in India's cloud and AI ecosystem. Microsoft announced a $3 billion commitment in January 2025 and an additional $17.5 billion investment later that year. MSFT stock gained 1.7% in morning trade, while retail sentiment on Stocktwits around the company dipped to ‘bullish’ from ‘extremely bullish’ over the past day. Chatter fell to ‘normal’ from ‘high’ levels. The company said the Hyderabad buildout gives it the “largest hyperscale cloud presence in India,” spanning three availability zones that Microsoft has previously described as roughly the size of two Eden Gardens cricket stadiums combined. Microsoft said the region is already seeing early customer adoption ahead of its broader rollout, with companies including Adani Group, Bajaj Finserv, HDFC Bank, and PB Pay using the infrastructure. Microsoft said Azure has posted strong double-digit growth in India over the past two years, with demand expected to increase further once the new cloud region becomes fully operational. Puneet Chandok, President of Microsoft India and South Asia, said customers are increasingly looking to move beyond AI experimentation toward deploying production-scale applications. "Whether it is a Frontier Firm already running AI at scale or an enterprise taking its first steps, the question we hear most often is: how do we move faster from experimenting with AI to creating durable business value with AI?" Chandok said. He added that the India South Central cloud region is a key part of Microsoft's strategy to provide the infrastructure, security and data sovereignty needed for enterprise AI adoption. The Hyderabad launch lands squarely in the middle of a broader hyperscaler buildout across India. Google confirmed a $15 billion data center project in Andhra Pradesh in October 2025, while AWS pledged $8.3 billion in India in January 2026, layered on top of an earlier $4.4 billion commitment tied to its second Indian cloud region, also based in Hyderabad. Microsoft currently operates four Azure regions in India directly, plus two more, Jio India West and Jio India Central, run in partnership with Reliance Jio. Globally, the company operates more than 80 cloud regions across 34 countries, backed by more than 500 data centers. The India expansion comes as all three hyperscalers are posting some of their strongest cloud growth numbers in years. In the June quarter, AWS generated $42.2 billion in revenue, an annualized run rate of $169 billion, growing 37% year-over-year. Microsoft's Intelligent Cloud segment, which includes Azure, produced $39.3 billion in quarterly revenue, an annualized run rate of $157 billion, with Azure itself growing 43% year-over-year. Google Cloud posted $24.8 billion in quarterly revenue, an annualized run rate of $99 billion, with growth accelerating sharply to 82% year-over-year from 63% the quarter before. Globally, AWS remains the largest cloud provider by revenue and holds roughly 28-31% of global cloud infrastructure market share, per Synergy Research Group, with Azure around 21% and Google Cloud around 14%. Shares of Unity Software Inc. (U) soared in Thursday’s opening trade after the company’s second-quarter (Q2) results surpassed Wall Street expectations. Unity reported earnings per share (EPS) of $0.28 in Q2 on revenue of $546.5 million, while Wall Street analysts expected an EPS of $0.25 on revenue of $514.2 million, according to Fiscal.ai data. Unity shares were up nearly 11% in the opening session. U was among the top trending tickers on Stocktwits at the time of writing. Unity CEO Matt Bromberg called the quarter "arguably the best" in the company’s history as a public company, crediting the continued success of the company's AI-powered Unity Vector platform and what he described as its strongest-ever product roadmap. “We're done looking backward. The flywheel we've constructed is spinning up, and we expect it to power us into the ranks of the most consequential companies of the AI era,” he said. Bromberg highlighted Unity Vector as a key growth engine, noting that the AI-powered advertising platform has surpassed a $1 billion annual revenue run rate two quarters ahead of schedule. He added that Unity recently began incorporating data from the roughly three billion people who play games built on the Unity runtime each month into Vector's AI models, calling it a long-term competitive advantage. Looking ahead, Unity forecast third-quarter strategic revenue of $540 million to $550 million and adjusted earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation, and amortization (EBITDA) of $185 million to $190 million, both above Q2 levels. Management said it expects a sixth consecutive quarter of adjusted EBITDA margin expansion, with margins projected to improve another 400 basis points sequentially. Chief Financial Officer Jarrod Yahes said Unity now expects to achieve GAAP net income profitability in the third quarter of 2026, one quarter earlier than previously anticipated. He added that the sale of the Supersonic business and the shutdown of the ironSource Ads network will improve margins in the second half of the year, leaving Unity “a more focused company positioned for faster revenue growth and dramatically higher levels of profitability.” Retail sentiment on Stocktwits around Unity trended in the ‘bullish’ territory with message volumes at ‘high’ levels. U stock is down 11% year-to-date, but up 23% over the past 12 months. Shares of Mirum Pharmaceuticals (MIRM) plummeted 15% in early trading on Thursday after the biotech firm disclosed a regulatory setback for its lead pipeline candidate, overshadowing better-than-expected second-quarter revenue and prompting Citizens to lower its price target. MIRM shares cracked the crucial 200-day moving average (200-DMA) for the first time since May 2025. Citizens lowered its price target to $137 from $146 while maintaining an ‘Outperform’ rating, citing an unexpected regulatory hurdle for its liver disease candidate Volixibat despite a strong second-quarter performance, according to The Fly. On Wednesday, CEO Chris Peetz said that following a pre-new drug application (NDA) meeting, the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) recommended conducting a Phase 3 study before a potential NDA submission, which Mirum now expects could occur in the first half of 2027. The firm said the FDA’s request for an additional Phase 3 trial of Volixibat in primary sclerosing cholangitis (PSC) is expected to delay the program and create near-term uncertainty. Volixibat has already received the FDA’s Breakthrough Therapy and Orphan Drug designations. Mirum reported a better-than-expected topline while also raising its full-year 2026 sales guidance. Revenue came in at $176.2 million, topping analysts’ estimates of $167.3 million, according to Fiscal.ai data. The company reported a wider-than-expected loss of $1.06 per share, compared with Wall Street’s forecast for a $0.76 per-share loss. Mirum ended the quarter with $561.3 million in cash, cash equivalents and investments and raised its full-year net product sales guidance to $680 million to $700 million, from its previous outlook of $660 million to $680 million. Uber Technologies (UBER) is drawing renewed attention after billionaire investor Bill Ackman backed a bullish investment case which argued that concerns over robotaxis have unfairly weighed on the stock’s valuation. Prominent investors believe that autonomous vehicles could become Uber’s biggest growth driver. UBER shares climbed 0.5% higher in pre-market trading on Thursday. Oguz Erkan, founder and writer of Capitalist-Letters, said that Uber is undervalued, trading at around 15 times expected 2027 earnings and 12 times 2028 earnings, despite expectations for double-digit annual growth through 2030. Erkan argued that Uber’s discounted valuation reflects investor concerns that robotaxis will hurt its future earnings, but he believes those fears are overdone. Erkan believes the autonomous vehicle market will remain fragmented, with players such as Waymo, Tesla, Zoox, and AVride. Rather than operating their own ride-hailing platforms, these companies could ultimately focus on being OEMs and supplying autonomous vehicles, while Uber continues serving as the platform connecting riders with fleets. “So, over time, we’ll see companies like Tesla and Waymo to position themselves as equipment providers (OEM) rather than service providers and platforms like Uber will act as service providers,” Erkan wrote in a post on X. He also argued that the capital-intensive nature of robotaxi fleets makes large-scale platform operators like Uber well positioned to benefit as adoption grows. Billionaire investor Bill Ackman, whose Pershing Square hedge fund disclosed a major stake in Uber in February 2025, said he agreed with the thesis. Meanwhile, Jason Calacanis, an angel investor in Uber, said the stock represented a “generational buying opportunity,” adding that the company’s valuation is now similar to Waymo’s. He also said the stock could climb back above $100 if Khosrowshahi successfully demonstrated 100 autonomous rides without a safety driver, to which Khosrowshahi replied: “We’re going to make it happen … and much more.” The comments came after Uber reiterated its plans to invest more than $10 billion in robotaxis over the coming years, primarily through equity investments in autonomous driving partners. CEO Dara Khosrowshahi also dismissed reports that Waymo could end its partnership with Uber, saying he expects the companies to continue working together in Austin and Atlanta while Uber expands relationships with other autonomous vehicle developers. Uber reported 12% revenue growth to $14.19 billion, although the figure missed analysts’ expectations of $14.27 billion, according to Fiscal.ai. However, earnings of $1.17 per share came above consensus estimates of $0.83 per share. On Thursday, Barclays trimmed its price target on Uber to $106 from $107 but maintained an ‘Overweight’ rating, saying the company is investing heavily to strengthen its position in autonomous vehicles and expand its global food delivery business. Wells Fargo also lowered its target to $89 from $100 while keeping an ‘Overweight’ rating. The brokerage said delivery demand remains strong and expects U.S. mobility to improve through 2026, although slower trip growth is weighing on the stock. DDOG stock fell as much as 20% in pre-market trade, on track to clock its largest single-day drop on record. According to Koyfin data, Datadog's previous biggest one-day drop was about 17.8% in March 2020. The move comes after DDOG stock hit an intra-day record high of over $292 in the previous session. Its value has more than doubled over the past year. The company reported earnings of $0.65 per share, beating Wall Street’s expectation of $0.58 earnings per share (EPS). Revenue came in at $1.12 billion, beating the consensus estimate of $1.08 billion, according to Koyfin. Datadog also reported strong growth in the quarter among “large customers.” The company ended the second quarter with about 4,720 customers contributing annual recurring revenue of more than $100,000, up from 3,850 customers last year. Looking ahead, Datadog forecast third-quarter (Q3) adjusted earnings between $0.63 and $0.65 per share on revenue of $1.135 billion to $1.145 billion. Analysts were expecting earnings of $0.61 per share and revenue of about $1.11 billion for the quarter. The company also lifted its full-year outlook. (INTC), Seagate Technology Holdings (STX), Western Digital Corp. (WDC), SanDisk Corp. (SNDK), and others in the sector declining between 3% and 16%. The Roundhill Memory ETF (DRAM) was down nearly 6% at the time of writing. The First Trust Nasdaq Semiconductor ETF (FTXL) declined about 2%. During an interview with CNBC, Frasse said that the current downturn and volatility in chip and memory stocks is just a reversion to the mean more than anything else. “At the end of the day, it appears that investors are looking for clear beats and guidance way outside of whatever the consensus is to really turn in the right direction,” he said. Over the long term, Frasse said that this downturn does not matter much for his firm, which is trying to keep its AI supercycle perspective in focus. “We think that the chip trade is still very strong, even if you’re seeing a little bit of volatility in the near term,” he added. Frasse added that he believes the AI trade cycle is still in the first third, while calling the technology transformative even though there is a lot of speculation around it. “From an adoption standpoint, I think that we’re still very low on the adoption side even though we hear about it every single day,” he said. Frasse believes that the full-fledged potential of AI has not been explored yet, and regardless of who wins the race and where the revenue comes from, at the end of the day, it’s chips that will power this industry. “In our eyes, there’s no world where we will need less compute, and we’re using less AI moving forward. At the end of the day, a lot of this is top-down noise,” he added. Despite concerns about memory supply constraints, Frasse believes that it is difficult to pinpoint the next bottleneck in AI. He added that while there is merit in concerns about memory being a bottleneck, he pointed to innovations in the industry such as High Bandwidth Memory (HBM) and High Bandwidth Flash (HBF) as attempts to ease these constraints. title: How Has Microsoft’s Story Changed In A Year? - Trefis
content: Microsoft’s management stressed Copilot and AI agents on its fiscal Q4 2026 call. The stock has returned 34% in three months, against 2.5% for the S&P 500. Microsoft (MSFT) needs fast Azure growth and revenue from Copilot’s paid seats to justify that gain. A year ago management led with a different topic, tied to a large part of Microsoft. What was it exactly? Microsoft used to highlight migrations, meaning customers moving their existing systems to the cloud. Azure is Microsoft’s cloud business. On the fiscal Q4 2025 call, held July 30, 2025, management said it saw “accelerating growth from migrations” again that quarter. Azure was already large when management said that. Azure had passed $75 billion in annual revenue, up 34%, management said on the same call. That was more than a quarter of Microsoft’s $281.7 billion of revenue in fiscal 2025. Migrations have had a smaller place in management’s remarks since then. On the fiscal Q2 2026 call, cloud migrations came up as just one example of progress outside AI. Microsoft’s management now leads with something else. Microsoft now leads with Copilot, its AI assistant, and with AI agents. Management reported over 30 million paid Microsoft 365 Copilot seats on the fiscal Q4 2026 call. Management also said pricing is moving from a fee per seat to a fee per seat plus a charge for usage. Copilot’s size in dollars is harder to see, because the figure management led with is a seat count. Microsoft 365 Copilot carries the Microsoft 365 name. So the nearest figure you have is the growth of the Microsoft 365 family. Commercial cloud revenue from Microsoft 365 grew 16% that quarter, after management adjusted for a lift in the year-earlier quarter. Azure grew 43% in the same quarter. Azure was part of the segment Microsoft reported as Intelligent Cloud. That segment brought in $39.3 billion of Microsoft’s $90 billion of revenue that quarter. Azure is still the faster grower after the change in what Microsoft leads with. Is Microsoft’s Change Of Emphasis A Problem For You? Microsoft’s change of emphasis is not a problem for you so far, because Azure is still growing fast. Management said on the fiscal Q4 2026 call that customer demand continues to exceed available capacity. By management’s account, Microsoft is short of capacity, not of customers. Copilot is the less certain part. You cannot read Copilot’s revenue from the 30 million seat count. You are paying 28.5 times a year of earnings for Microsoft stock, against 21.7 times for the S&P 500. If Azure slows before Copilot’s revenue can be seen in the reported figures, that higher price would be hard to justify. You will see Azure’s next figure in the fiscal Q1 2027 report. Management guided Azure growth of approximately 45% for that quarter, before currency effects. If Azure comes in well below that guide, the smaller role for migrations becomes a concern. Microsoft said on September 2, 2026 that it will start reporting Azure sales each quarter. Azure will be easier to follow once that reporting starts. Copilot’s paid seats are still a count, not a revenue figure. You can look for a hint of that revenue in the same fiscal Q1 2027 report. Microsoft 365 commercial cloud growth above that adjusted 16% could be an early sign of Copilot’s paid seats lifting revenue growth. title: Which Dates Could Move Microsoft Stock Most? - Trefis
content: Microsoft (MSFT) stock has gained about 34% in three months, and you may wonder whether it can hold that gain. Management expects about $175 billion of capital spending in calendar 2026 and has said the spending may lower operating margins. A few dated events will show whether that spending is paying off. Below are the earnings reports and other dates most likely to move Microsoft stock over the next six months. Microsoft is scheduled to report earnings on October 27, 2026. The report covers fiscal Q1 2027. Azure, its cloud computing business, is the part of that report most likely to move the stock. Azure was reported in the Intelligent Cloud segment, which brought in $39.3 billion of the $90 billion in fiscal Q4 2026 revenue. Management guided on the July 29, 2026 call to Azure growth of about 45%. That guide was for fiscal Q1 2027 and excludes currency effects. Customer demand still exceeds available capacity, management said. The number to watch on October 27, 2026 is the Azure growth rate. A rate below about 45% would mean Azure fell short of that guide. title: Microsoft's AI Spending Didn't Change—Wall Street's View of It Did - MarketBeat
content:
Microsoft NASDAQ: MSFT investors have owned two different companies in 2026. Or at least, they've been told two very different stories about the same one. But in the second half, the story is about discipline. Microsoft shares rose more than 36% in the last three months and turned positive for the year. It's a remarkable comeback for a stock that had fallen 20%. The reason why may come as a surprise. The same capital spending that scared investors in the spring has become a selling point. To illustrate that point, CNBC's Jeff Marks now calls Microsoft "one of the few hyperscalers that is living within their means." So what actually changed? Less than you might think. The business was improving the whole time. What flipped was the narrative investors used to interpret it. Here's how the change in sentiment happened, and what the chart says about what comes next. Microsoft's fourth quarter of fiscal 2026 ran from April through June, which is the exact stretch when the stock slid toward its lows. But the Q4 earnings report showed that during those same three months, Microsoft was delivering results on Copilot, which had been considered a major obstacle. Microsoft ended the quarter with 30 million paid Copilot seats, up 10 million in a single quarter and the fastest seat growth since Copilot launched. Q4 revenue increased 18% year-over-year to reach $90 billion. In other words, customers were buying Copilot at a record pace. At the same time, investors were dumping the stock on fears that nobody would. Investors simply didn't have the data yet. Spending tells the same story. Earlier this year, Microsoft's data center budget was treated as a liability. Investors questioned whether hyperscalers could generate sufficient returns on their enormous AI investments. Microsoft didn't slash spending to win them back. Instead, it brought more capacity online, delivered 43% revenue growth from Azure and other cloud services, and remained free cash flow positive. That's the key point. Capital expenditure (CapEx) didn't change. The return on investment story did. Once investors saw capacity turning into revenue, "reckless" became "disciplined." Analysts followed the price. Stifel upgraded MSFT from Hold to Buy on Sept. 22, arguing that the company had decisively turned a corner. Then came the Copilot redesign on Sept. 25. On Wednesday, Sept. 30, Piper Sandler raised its price target to $610 from $550 while maintaining an Overweight rating, saying the Copilot narrative had “improved materially” this year. Those upgrades arrived after the stock had rallied more than 40% off its lows. That's how sentiment changes work. Analyst consensus confirms a move. It rarely starts one. After the post-earnings move, Microsoft has spent about two months trading mostly between $485 and $520. Meanwhile, the 50-day simple moving average has climbed steeply to about $480. That's a constructive setup. Price is digesting its gains while the trend catches up underneath it. Momentum has cooled, though. The MACD line sits at 7.02, just below its signal line at 7.35. The histogram is only slightly negative. Put simply, the stock isn't overheated. It's resting. A MACD crossover back above the signal line would suggest the consolidation is resolving higher. If that happens, the next major test is the 52-week high near $554. On the downside, the rising 50-day average near $480 is the level to watch. Sentiment whiplash cuts both ways. Investors who sold near $355 on a bad story can just as easily overpay on a good one. The macro backdrop deserves respect, too. The 10-year Treasury yield advanced to 5.25%, its highest level since 2007. That puts pressure on big tech valuations. The next chapter of this story will be written in usage data. The more advanced Cowork, Code, and Autopilot features shift to usage-based pricing. That's the metric to watch when Microsoft reports again in late October. Microsoft didn't become a great business in August. It was already one in June. The only thing that changed was how investors chose to tell the story. That's the real lesson for patient investors. Narratives swing quickly, while fundamentals compound quietly. The next time the story around Microsoft turns, check whether the numbers do too. title: MSFT Stock Slides 4.5% — Microsoft Price Target Revision By Stifel And Xbox Pricing Changes In Focus - Stocktwits
content: Shares of Microsoft Corp. (MSFT) fell nearly 4.5% during Thursday afternoon’s trading session. The decline came after Stifel revised its outlook on Microsoft amid updated profitability expectations, alongside the company’s announcement of higher Xbox prices driven by rising memory chip costs. The MSFT stock ended Thursday's session down 3.66%. In after-hours trading, the shares pared some of those losses and were up 0.22% at the time of writing. Stifel lowered its price target on Microsoft to $400 from $415, while maintaining a Hold rating on the stock. The revised target still implies around 9% upside from MSFT’s Wednesday’s close. The firm said following Oracle’s (ORCL) recent earnings and gross margin guidance, it reviewed Microsoft’s FY27 sell-side gross margin estimates and said they appear too high, reported TheFly. According to data from Koyfin, 53 of the 56 analysts covering MSFT rate it ‘Buy’ or ‘Strong buy,’ while 3 rate it ‘Hold.’ The 12-month average target on the stock is $561.11, suggesting about 42% upside from the latest close. Microsoft said Xbox console prices will increase worldwide starting August 1, with 512 GB models going up by $100 and 1 TB versions rising by $150. The company also confirmed it will discontinue its 2 TB model as part of a broader lineup change. Microsoft said in a blog post that storage and memory costs have surged sharply, forcing the pricing move despite months of negotiations with suppliers. The company added that console storage and memory prices have risen more than 2.5 times, with expectations of further increases ahead. Microsoft said that it had previously raised Xbox prices in October and had hoped further increases would not be necessary. But ongoing supply constraints are impacting the entire consumer electronics industry, with consoles particularly affected. Earlier in the day, Apple also raised prices across its MacBook and iPad lineup, citing higher memory and storage costs amid strong AI-driven demand. CEO Tim Cook said the price increases were becoming unavoidable despite efforts to shield customers. Responding to Microsoft’s Xbox price hikes and Apple’s higher MacBooks and iPad prices, The Kobeissi Letter, which provides market commentary, said in a post on X on Thursday that “AI-induced price hikes have begun.” The post also detailed updated Xbox pricing, stating that the Series S 1TB has risen $150 to $599, the Series X 1TB has increased $150 to $799, the Series S 512GB has moved up $100 to $499, and the Series X 1TB Digital edition has risen $150 to $749. (AAPL) dropped nearly 6.5% on Thursday afternoon after the company announced price hikes on MacBooks and iPads due to a memory crunch. Munster said in a post on X, “$AAPL trading down 5% on the news of an average Mac weighted price increase of about 17% (factoring in mix) feels like an overreaction on fears of demand destruction.” He adds that the market is underestimating Apple’s pricing power and ecosystem strength. “My take is for the most part, demand for Apple products are inelastic, that is a large change in price has a smaller change in demand,” Munster wrote, pointing to his estimate of Apple’s 1.5 billion consumers who remain deeply embedded in its ecosystem. According to Munster, Apple users continue to derive strong value even after price increases, limiting the risk of meaningful demand erosion. He also highlighted the long replacement cycle for Macs, stating, “Average life of a Mac is 4.5 years before it’s traded in which means a $200 increase adds $3.70 a month to the cost of ownership.” While acknowledging that customers may have to absorb higher upfront costs, Munster suggested behavior is unlikely to change materially. “Rational buyers likely will be frustrated and buy anyway,” he added, highlighting his view that the selloff reflects sentiment rather than fundamentals. Apple raised prices across its MacBook and iPad lineup on Thursday, citing higher memory and storage costs driven by surging AI demand. CEO Tim Cook said in an interview with The Wall Street Journal that price hikes were becoming unavoidable despite efforts to protect customers. “We’ve been trying to shield our customers from the increases, but the situation has become unsustainable,” Cook said. title: How Much Upside Is Left In Microsoft Stock? - Trefis
content: Microsoft (MSFT) shares returned 37% over the past three months, against 2.6% for the S&P 500. Even so, Microsoft’s P/E, the price divided by a year of profit, is 28.3. That is below 31.8, the stock’s average at the last twelve quarter-ends, leaving out readings above 100. A run that big makes buyers wary, but the shares cost less per dollar of profit than usual. So how much upside is left in Microsoft stock at today’s price? On the assumptions below, Microsoft stock would be worth about $753 a share in three years. That is 48% above today’s price of $508.96. Spread over three years, the gain works out to about 14% a year. The scenario is arithmetic on the company’s own numbers, not a forecast. In this scenario, revenue grows 15.1% a year, a little below the 17.8% of the twelve months to fiscal Q4 2026. The table below sets today’s figures beside the scenario’s figures three years out. All of the gain comes from Microsoft selling more. The P/E is held flat by assumption, and the gain is trimmed a little by a slightly lower net margin. In fiscal 2026, Microsoft’s fastest-growing segment was Intelligent Cloud, which includes the Azure cloud computing service. Revenue from Azure and other cloud services grew 43% in fiscal Q4 2026. So far, yes. Management said on the fiscal Q4 2026 call that customer demand still exceeds available capacity. Microsoft also said it remains on track to roughly double its overall capacity in two years. Copilot, Microsoft’s AI assistant, is the other product Microsoft is selling more of. By the fiscal Q4 2026 call, paid Microsoft 365 Copilot seats had passed 30 million. NHS England, for example, is rolling out Copilot to 505,000 clinicians and staff. Microsoft is also moving from charging per seat to charging per seat plus usage. Customers have signed $678 billion of commercial contracts that Microsoft has not yet booked as revenue. The part of that total excluding OpenAI grew 25%. Management gave no full-year revenue figure for fiscal 2027, only a call for another year of double-digit growth. Management also expects a slightly lower operating margin in fiscal 2027 as it spends on capacity. The table below shows the three-year upside when one assumption changes and the other two stay as they are. The upside is smallest if the net margin falls back to its three-year average. The margin has room to fall because today’s net margin matches its highest level in ten years. With the P/E and margin as assumed, three years of owning the stock would return nothing if revenue grew 1.0% a year. That is 16.8 points below the pace of the last twelve months. Microsoft’s slowest annual revenue growth in the last three fiscal years was 14.9%. Revenue growth is where Microsoft’s upside comes from. Yet growth can fall a long way from its recent pace before owning the stock returns nothing. The case stays intact as long as customer demand keeps exceeding the capacity Microsoft can supply. If revenue growth slows sharply, Microsoft becomes a riskier bet that relies more on its margin staying near its ten-year high. Before you decide on MSFT, consider a better choice.  moved into the spotlight on Wednesday as American stocks edged higher and artificial intelligence enthusiasm once again powered the technology sector. The software and cloud giant benefited from a supportive tone across large platform companies, with semiconductors and AI infrastructure names extending recent strength and drawing attention to the spending wave behind cloud computing. Market commentary tied the company's momentum to its recent redesign of the Copilot application, which brings the full functionality of Word, Excel and PowerPoint into a single assistant experience. The update also introduces a new home starting point that combines chat with an agentic tool capable of carrying out multi-step tasks, a feature set that market watchers see as central to the company's AI story. The advance came as other parts of the market lagged. Financials were among the weakest sectors of September, energy softened as crude eased, and healthcare traded roughly flat. In that setting, technology once again carried the market, and Microsoft stood out as one of the household names whose product news and infrastructure plans shaped the conversation. The redesigned Copilot represents a deliberate effort to move beyond simple chat. By placing document creation, spreadsheet work and presentation building inside the assistant, Microsoft aims to make the tool the front door to everyday productivity. Users can start a task in natural language and see it carried through familiar applications without switching context. Agentic capabilities are the most closely watched piece. Instead of merely answering questions, an agent can plan a sequence of actions, gather information, draft content and complete steps on behalf of the user. Enterprise buyers are keen to understand how reliably such tools can operate, and how they can be governed inside large organisations with strict data rules. The update also brings natural language coding tools into the experience, widening the audience beyond professional developers. Business users can describe an automation in plain language and let the assistant generate the underlying logic. Supporters say that could democratise software creation, while sceptics point to questions about accuracy, oversight and security. Reports of a large data-centre buildout have added another layer to the day's discussion. Microsoft has been expanding capacity across many regions to serve demand for Azure, its cloud platform, and for the AI services that run on top of it. Land, power, cooling, networking and advanced chips are all part of a sprawling construction effort. The scale of spending has become a central debate among market watchers. Supporters argue that customers are clamouring for compute and that capacity constraints have limited growth, so building ahead is prudent. Critics ask whether revenue from AI services will grow fast enough to justify such heavy capital expenditure, and whether cash generation will remain robust in the meantime. Power availability is emerging as a defining constraint across the industry. Utilities, developers and technology firms are negotiating long-term arrangements, exploring new generation sources and rethinking site selection. Microsoft's ability to secure energy and equipment on favourable terms is therefore becoming as important to its cloud ambitions as software design itself. Microsoft operates across three broad areas: productivity and business processes, intelligent cloud, and personal computing. Productivity includes the Office applications, Dynamics, LinkedIn and related services. The cloud segment centres on Azure, server products and enterprise support. Personal computing covers Windows, devices, Xbox gaming and search advertising. The breadth of the portfolio gives the company an unusually diversified base. Enterprise subscriptions deliver recurring revenue, cloud consumption grows with customer workloads, and gaming and consumer software supply additional streams. That mix has helped the company weather cycles that have hit narrower competitors harder. Enterprise relationships are the foundation of the model. Large organisations often standardise on Microsoft tools for email, collaboration, security, identity and data management, and that installed presence gives the company a natural channel to introduce new AI features. Each product cycle therefore builds upon customer trust that has been developed over decades. Azure competes with Amazon Web Services and Google Cloud for the workloads of enterprises, governments and start-ups. The contest has intensified as artificial intelligence changes what customers ask of cloud providers, moving the conversation from storage and basic computing to training, inference and specialised model services. Microsoft's partnership with OpenAI has been a major differentiator, giving Azure customers access to leading models and giving the model developer a large-scale computing home. The relationship has evolved over time, and market watchers follow its terms closely because of implications for capacity, exclusivity and revenue sharing. The company has also broadened its model catalogue, supporting offerings from several developers and building its own in-house models. That flexibility appeals to customers who wish to avoid dependence on a single supplier, and it positions Azure as a marketplace for intelligence rather than a single-model shop. A recurring question in market commentary is how quickly AI features convert into paid usage. Businesses have run pilots for many months, and the pace of wider rollouts depends on proven productivity gains, integration effort and the comfort of compliance teams. Some organisations have moved decisively, while others are proceeding cautiously. Pricing structures remain a topic of experimentation. Per-user subscriptions, consumption-based charges and bundled tiers all coexist, and the company is refining packaging to match different customer needs. The pattern will shape how the value of AI capabilities is captured across the existing software base. Feedback from early users has generally highlighted time savings on drafting, summarising and data tasks, alongside concerns about occasional errors. Microsoft has responded with governance features, grounding methods and audit tools designed to reassure regulated industries. Progress on those fronts will influence how widely the tools spread inside large employers. Large technology companies are in the middle of a spending supercycle. Cloud providers, chip designers and equipment makers are all responding to demand for AI compute, and that wave has reshaped earnings expectations across the group. Today's strength in semiconductors and infrastructure names fits neatly with the storyline surrounding Microsoft. The bluechip stocks universe includes many companies that combine global scale with strong balance sheets, and Microsoft is often described as a bellwether among them. Its results are widely read as a gauge of enterprise technology budgets, making its commentary influential well beyond its own share price. At the same time, market watchers have become more discerning about which spending will pay off. Companies that can show a clear link between infrastructure outlays and customer demand tend to receive a warmer reception, while those with vague plans face tougher questions. That scrutiny is healthy for the sector and frames coverage of each new announcement. Microsoft's competitors span nearly every segment it serves. In productivity software, Google Workspace and a range of specialised tools contend for users. In cloud, Amazon and Google are formidable rivals. In gaming, Sony and Nintendo compete for players, and in security, dedicated cybersecurity firms challenge its offerings. In artificial intelligence, the field is crowded with model developers, chipmakers and application companies. Some rivals emphasise open models, others focus on consumer assistants, and still others build vertical solutions for particular industries. Microsoft's strategy is to embed intelligence across its existing products and surface it through Azure for developers. Competitive intensity is unlikely to fade. Every major platform is racing to attach assistants and agents to daily workflows, and success will likely depend on distribution, trust, reliability and cost. Microsoft's ubiquity in the workplace gives it an advantage in distribution, but it must keep proving that its tools deliver dependable results. Regulators around the world are paying closer attention to artificial intelligence, cloud concentration and software bundling. European authorities in particular have examined how large platforms package products and how cloud licensing terms affect competitors. Outcomes could influence contracts, product design and pricing over time. Cybersecurity is another persistent challenge. As software becomes more powerful and connected, the consequences of vulnerabilities grow. Microsoft has committed substantial resources to secure development and threat detection, yet the scale of its footprint makes it a constant focus for sophisticated attackers. Energy, supply chains and talent also present hurdles. Building AI capacity requires scarce chips, transformers and skilled engineers, and shortages can delay projects. The company's ability to navigate those constraints will be one of the defining operational tests of the coming period. The Copilot announcement arrived alongside continuing reports of new data-centre projects, creating a combined narrative of product momentum and infrastructure expansion. Trading commentary described the reaction as constructive, with the shares rising as market participants weighed the strategic implications. The stock had recovered strongly over recent months after earlier concerns about capital spending and competition. Sentiment improved as customer demand for cloud services stayed firm and as AI features began to appear in more enterprise agreements. The recovery has made the company a focal point in discussions of which names are setting the pace within the technology group. Even so, the day-to-day tone remains sensitive to news about capital expenditure, model partnerships and competitive launches. Market watchers expect volatility to persist as fresh data arrives, especially around quarterly reporting and major developer conferences where new capabilities are unveiled. Microsoft is regarded as one of the most financially robust companies in the world, with formidable cash generation and a top-tier credit standing. That strength allows it to fund ambitious infrastructure programmes, pursue acquisitions and maintain regular distributions to owners of the stock even while spending heavily on capacity. The balance between growth spending and financial discipline is under permanent review. Market watchers ask how depreciation from new data centres will influence margins, how quickly cloud revenue will scale and whether efficiency gains elsewhere can offset the costs. Management has generally pledged to align spending with demand signals. The company's diversified revenue also provides ballast. Even if one segment slows, subscription software, security services and gaming can offer steadier contributions. That resilience is a key reason the stock is regarded as a core position in many diversified portfolios despite periodic bouts of volatility. Microsoft has emphasised responsible development of artificial intelligence, publishing principles and building internal review processes for new products. Leaders describe the goal as balancing rapid innovation with safeguards around privacy, fairness and security, a balance that matters greatly to enterprise customers and regulators. Culture has also been a talking point since the company shifted toward a growth mindset under its current chief executive. Collaboration, learning and customer focus are repeatedly cited as reasons for its long run of strong execution, and the approach is often studied by other large organisations. Microsoft's size means its performance influences the tone of major benchmarks. When the stock climbs alongside chipmakers and other AI names, it reinforces the market narrative of technology strength; when it stalls, questions about spending and monetisation move to the foreground. The coming weeks bring quarterly reporting season, when the company will update the market on cloud growth, AI adoption and capital plans. Commentary on capacity constraints, customer demand and partnership arrangements is likely to be scrutinised for hints about the pace of expansion. For those following large American companies, the day underlines how interlinked the technology chain has become. Software, cloud, chips, power and construction now move in tandem more often than before, and a single product announcement can echo across many sectors of the market. Beyond productivity and cloud, Microsoft maintains a sizeable gaming business anchored by Xbox, its subscription service and a catalogue of studios acquired in recent years. Gaming provides a consumer-facing counterweight to the enterprise focus and creates a large audience for cloud streaming and AI-assisted development tools. Security has become a major growth engine as organisations look for integrated defences. The company bundles identity, endpoint protection, cloud security and threat intelligence, and it uses its enormous telemetry to spot emerging attacks. Customers value consolidation, and that trend gives Microsoft an advantage over point-solution vendors. LinkedIn and Dynamics add further breadth, giving the company a presence in professional networking, recruiting, sales and customer service software. Each of these units can absorb AI features, creating additional routes to monetise the same underlying models across many workflows. Developers are a critical constituency for any platform, and Microsoft has cultivated them through GitHub, Visual Studio and its cloud tools. AI-assisted coding has become one of the earliest and most tangible uses of generative models, and the company has been able to weave those features directly into daily programming routines. The extension of natural language coding to a broader audience within Copilot could widen that ecosystem further. If business users can produce simple applications and automations without traditional programming, demand for the underlying platforms and data services could expand. The idea is closely watched by market participants and competitors alike. An active developer base also acts as a moat. Tools, extensions, documentation and community knowledge accumulate over years and are hard for rivals to replicate. Microsoft's standing with developers helps ensure that new AI capabilities reach customers quickly and are built into real-world applications. title: AMZN, MSFT, GOOGL Need $1 Trillion in Revenue To Earn 15% Return on AI Capex — Here's What Goldman Says About Their $1.69 Trillion Backlog - TradingView
content: Amazon.com Inc. AMZN, Microsoft Corp. MSFT, and Alphabet Inc. GOOG GOOGL require $1 trillion in combined revenue between 2028 and 2030 to achieve a 15% return on invested capital for artificial intelligence infrastructure. However, these companies’ existing cloud service backlogs total $1.69 trillion, covering 59% of that required revenue. To justify upfront capital expenditures on AI infrastructure, U.S.-Based hyperscalers must meet specific future revenue thresholds. According to a financial framework published by Goldman Sachs Global Investment Research, the path to profitability is supported by current revenue pipelines. Summarizing the data, Futurum Equites’ Shay Boloor noted on X that “Goldman says $AMZN, $MSFT and $GOOGL only need ~$1T of 2028 to 2030 revenue to earn a 15% ROIC on AI capex.” This $1 trillion revenue target represents the amount needed over a three-year period to hit the 15% Return on Invested Capital (ROIC) threshold. Goldman says $AMZN, $MSFT and $GOOGL only need ~$1T of 2028 to 2030 revenue to earn a 15% ROIC on AI capex. That’s just ~60% of the ~$1.7T backlog already on the books which makes AI buildout look a lot less speculative with even more upside if utilization or pricing moves… pic.twitter.com/Y26EL041x9 Read Also:  AI or Chatbots Face Criminal Charges in 2026? Crypto Bettors Weigh the Odds Financial models indicate that existing contractual commitments provide a foundation for these capital investments. The three companies reported a combined backlog of $1,687.9 billion as of the second calendar quarter of 2026. According to the graphic shared by Boloor, Microsoft leads with a reported backlog of $678 billion, followed by Amazon at $513.9 billion, and Google at $496 billion. According to Goldman’s analysis, Microsoft would need to convert about 39.6% of its current backlog into revenue, compared with 67.7% for Amazon and 77.7% for Google, to meet their respective shares of the $1 trillion 2028-2030 revenue requirement. Backlog figures reflect Goldman Sachs’ proprietary Calendar Quarter (CQ2’26) normalization and estimates, which may differ from reported company SEC filings. The ratio of required revenue to current backlog alters the perceived risk of ongoing data center expansions. Analysis of the Goldman Sachs data emphasizes this buffer, with Boloor saying: “That’s just ~60% of the ~$1.7T backlog already on the books, which makes AI buildout look a lot less speculative with even more upside if utilization or pricing moves higher.” The underlying framework calculates these returns assuming 29 gigawatts of implied capacity added, factoring in utilization rates scaling to 85% by the year 2030.
